label: L3
title: Harnessing the Power of Analytics in an Organizational Context
brief: Class 3 argues that change management is a core capability of T-shaped analytics professionals and supplies the frameworks to see why. Subramaniam's four tiers of digital transformation run from operational efficiencies and advanced operational efficiencies (data useful for existing products/services) to data-driven services from value chains and data-driven products and services (products/services useful for data), illustrated by Michelin and OCP. Representations are built from frames of interpretation, the present context and intentions; deduction works within an existing representation (Type 1 change: efficiency, optimization) while induction builds new ones (Type 2 change: new business logic and mindset), and the number-sequence puzzles show that induction is never certain. The economics of tangibles (positive marginal cost, capacity limits, diminishing returns, Marshall's equilibrium) differ from those of intangibles (near-zero marginal cost, network effects, increasing returns, winner-takes-all), and falling transaction costs move Coase's firm boundary, deconstructing value chains into platforms and ecosystems. The OCP case shows a state-owned phosphate company in 2006 with weak financial performance, a pension 'ticking bomb' and a rock-heavy position while the market moved toward fertilizers, held back by biases such as pain-avoiding denial and framing, and then growing through new S-curves supported by analytics, from a 600,000-constraint MILP for business steering to digital agriculture services.
kp: Change management is a core capability of T-shaped profiles; digital leadership builds the digital culture and develops T-shaped employees.
Four tiers (Subramaniam): operational efficiencies, advanced operational efficiencies, data-driven services from value chains, data-driven products and services.
'Data useful for products/services' enhances existing offerings; 'products/services useful for data' creates new offerings from the data existing products generate (e.g. Michelin Tire-as-a-Service).
Representations of a complex situation come from frames of interpretation, the present context and intentions, and drive actions, decisions and behaviors (Genelot).
Type 1 change = within the same system of representations (efficiency, optimization; deduction). Type 2 = change of the representations themselves (new business logic and mindset; induction).
Induction is fallible: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 continues as 32 (powers of 2) or 31 (circle regions cut by chords between n points).

Tangibles: positive marginal cost, capacity limits, diminishing returns, cost-based prices, several firms coexist. Intangibles: near-zero marginal cost, network effects, increasing returns, winner takes all.
Metcalfe: network value ∝ $n^2$; the data network effect loops usage → data → knowledge of preferences → better products → more usage.
Coase: firms exist because using the market is costly; connectivity, open standards and AI agents cut transaction costs, move the firm boundary and deconstruct value chains into platforms/ecosystems.
OCP 2006–07: ~45% of rock and ~46% of acid trade but <10% of fertilizers while the market shifted downstream; framing and denial blocked options such as moving ammonia production to Jorf.

topics.x: The T-profile combines depth in advanced analytics with breadth in strategy, business model, operating model and change management, on top of a data/digital mindset, which makes change management a core capability. Digital leadership enables a digital culture and develops employees into T-shaped professionals; managers and employees must build digital skills and adapt to new ways of working (Peter & Lindeque).

Subramaniam's tiers are (1) operational efficiencies, (2) advanced operational efficiencies, (3) data-driven services from value chains and (4) data-driven products and services. The lower tiers use data to enhance existing products/services; the upper tiers use products/services to generate data for new offerings, such as Michelin's connected tires and Tire-as-a-Service or OCP's digital agriculture and plant-nutrition services, which raise the question of what new products and services farm data can unlock.

topics.n: Representations, induction and Type 1 vs Type 2 change
topics.x: Genelot's representations' construction system: frames of interpretation (culture, values, beliefs, paradigms, experience, training, knowledge), the present context (pressures, constraints, risks, geo-economic and social factors) and intentions/ambition shape how a complex situation is represented, and representations drive actions, decisions and behaviors. Type 1 change happens within the same system of representations (efficiency, optimization) and is paired with deduction; Type 2 change alters the representations themselves (new business logic and mindset) and is paired with induction. Sequences such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 → 32 or 31 show that induction from the same data can support different rules.

Tangibles have positive marginal cost, economies of scale, capacity constraints and diminishing returns; Marshall's world has an optimal plant size, several coexisting firms, cost-based prices and a predictable equilibrium. Intangibles have near-zero marginal cost, are non-rival and scalable, and show network effects and increasing returns, which lead to winner-takes-all, monopoly-like structures (Arthur, 1996). Metcalfe's law (value ∝ $n^2$) and the data network effect amplify this, and the Starbucks ladder ($0.07 beans to a $4.50 latte experience) shows value moving from tangible to intangible.

Porter's value chain and five forces assume company and industry boundaries. Coase (1937) explains why firms exist: using the market is costly (finding a supplier, writing and enforcing contracts), so the boundary sits where the marginal cost of organizing inside equals the marginal cost of transacting with the market. The hidden assumption is high transaction costs; connectivity, open standards and AI agents lower them, moving the boundary and deconstructing value chains into platforms and ecosystems (Choudary, Reshuffle, 2025).

topics.n: OCP case: from a 2006 diagnosis to analytics at scale
topics.x: OCP turns phosphate rock into phosphoric acid and fertilizers. In 2006 it was a state office with an export royalty that gave the government shareholder poor incentives, weak financial performance, a pension fund called 'a ticking bomb', and market shares of ~45% in rock, ~46% in acid but <10% in fertilizers while trade shifted toward processed products; Kroll found no corruption, just an aging company with no real industrial and commercial strategy. Growth then came through new S-curves supported by analytics: a daily multi-period MILP with about 600,000 constraints and 500,000 variables (60,000 binary) for business steering, and customized fertilization made possible by $1 LIBS soil analysis and high-resolution soil mapping.

The lecture lists functional fixedness, confirmation bias, anchoring, framing, pain-avoiding psychological denial, social conformity, sunk cost and theory-induced blindness (after Kahneman and Munger). At OCP, pushback against 'strategic retreat' reflected pain-avoiding denial, and decades spent on consolidating the cliff or trucking ammonia at Safi reflected framing, until a study showed that moving ammonia production to Jorf removed the risk and generated more profit.

quiz.q: In Subramaniam's framework, what is tier 4?
o: Data-driven products and services
Operational efficiencies
Advanced operational efficiencies
Data-driven services from value chains
quiz.e: The order is 1 operational efficiencies, 2 advanced operational efficiencies, 3 data-driven services from value chains, 4 data-driven products and services.

quiz.q: Michelin charges fleet customers per kilometer and uses real-time tire data to optimize fleet performance. Which side of the four-tier framework is this?
o: Products/services useful for data: a new service built on data generated by existing products
Data useful for products/services: enhancing the existing tire
Operational efficiency in tire manufacturing
Not data-driven, since tires are physical products
quiz.e: Tire-as-a-Service is a new offering built on data from the product in use. Optimizing tire formulations and production would be data used to enhance the existing product.

quiz.q: OCP uses its optimization model to cut shipping costs within its existing business model. Which type of change is this?
o: Type 1: change within the same system of representations (efficiency/optimization)
Type 2: change of the underlying representations
Both, because a new tool is involved
Neither, because nothing changes for customers
quiz.e: Optimization inside the current business logic is Type 1. Type 2 requires a new business logic and mindset, such as moving into digital agriculture services.

o: A new business logic and mindset
Efficiency and optimization
Incremental cost cutting
Deductive reasoning within the current model
quiz.e: The slides contrast Type 1 (efficiency/optimization) with Type 2 (new business logic and mindset); deduction is paired with Type 1.

quiz.q: Sequence: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. If the rule is 'number of regions a circle is cut into by chords between n points on it', what comes next?
quiz.e: The circle-division count runs 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31. 32 is the powers-of-2 rule; the point is that the same observations support different rules, so induction is never certain.

quiz.q: Sequence: 1, 2, 3, 5, ?. What does the Fibonacci rule $u_{n+2} = u_{n+1} + u_n$ give?
quiz.e: 3 + 5 = 8. The slide's other continuation, 7, follows the prime-number reading of the same sequence.

quiz.q: Which pair belongs to the economics of intangibles?
o: Near-zero marginal cost and increasing returns
Capacity constraints and diminishing returns
Positive marginal cost and economies of scale
Cost-based pricing and an optimal plant size
quiz.e: Intangibles: near-zero marginal cost, non-rival and scalable, network effects, increasing returns. The other options describe tangibles and Marshall's world.

quiz.q: In Marshall's world of diminishing returns, what market structure results?
o: Several firms coexist at an optimal plant size, with prices based on cost
One firm takes all or most of the market
Prices fall toward zero as users grow
Network effects lock customers into one platform
quiz.e: Firms that get ahead eventually run into limitations, so a predictable equilibrium of prices and shares emerges. Winner-takes-all is the increasing-returns world of information goods.

quiz.q: By Metcalfe's law (value ∝ $n^2$), a platform that grows from 1 million to 3 million users increases its network value by about:
quiz.e: (3/1)^2 = 9. 3× is linear growth, which is exactly the tangible-economy intuition that network effects break; 27× would be a cubic law.

quiz.q: On the Starbucks ladder, a $4.50 latte is roughly how many times the $0.07 cost of the ~10g of beans in it?
o: About 64×
About 19×
About 4×
About 6.4×
quiz.e: 4.50 / 0.07 ≈ 64. 19× compares the latte with roasted retail coffee ($0.24) and ~4× with counter-served coffee ($1.20), not with the commodity.

quiz.q: A recommender suggests 'what users similar to you liked'. Which approach is this, and which loop does it feed?
o: Collaborative filtering; the data network effect (more usage → more data → better products → more usage)
Content-based filtering; economies of scale in production
Collaborative filtering; diminishing returns to data
Content-based filtering; Metcalfe's law on items
quiz.e: Collaborative filtering is based on user similarity; content-based filtering is based on item similarity. Better recommendations bring more usage and more data, the data network effect.

quiz.q: What is Coase's 1937 answer to 'why do firms exist?'
o: Using the market is costly: finding suppliers, writing and enforcing contracts
Production has economies of scale
Taxes favor large organizations
Network effects reward size
quiz.e: Firms internalize activities until the marginal cost of organizing inside equals the marginal cost of transacting with the market.

quiz.q: Connectivity, open standards and AI agents sharply lower the cost of transacting with the market. Under Coase's logic, what happens?
o: The boundary moves toward fewer activities inside the firm, opening the value chain to platforms and ecosystems
More activities move inside the firm, because market transactions become relatively costlier
The boundary does not move, because it depends only on economies of scale
Industry boundaries harden and protect incumbents
quiz.e: A lower market-transaction cost meets the internal organizing cost at fewer in-house activities, so the firm boundary moves (old vs new boundary) and value chains deconstruct into platforms and ecosystems. The second option reverses the direction of the cost change.

quiz.q: OCP's daily optimization model has about 500,000 variables, of which 60,000 are binary. What share of the variables is binary?
quiz.e: 60,000 / 500,000 = 0.12. 10% divides by the 600,000 constraints instead of the variables, and 88% is the continuous share.

quiz.q: Moving soil prescriptions from a 2.5-acre grid to TerraBlaster's 0.4-acre grid multiplies the number of zones per field by about:
quiz.e: 2.5 / 0.4 = 6.25 zones per old zone. 2.1 is the difference in acres, 0.16 is the inverse ratio, and 40% is the share of a field that gets a sub-optimal dose under the coarse grid.

quiz.q: In 2007 OCP held about 45% of rock trade, 46% of phosphoric acid and under 10% of fertilizers, while traded phosphate shifted away from raw rock. Which diagnosis follows?
o: Weak downstream presence: OCP was strongest where the market was shrinking and weakest where it was growing
Over-integration into fertilizers at the expense of mining
Strong downstream position but weak upstream supply
Corruption, as the 2006 Kroll audit concluded
quiz.e: The share of rock in global phosphate exports was falling and players were integrating, yet OCP was barely present in fertilizers. Kroll found no malpractice or corruption, only an aging company without a real industrial and commercial strategy.

quiz.q: At Safi, decades of options focused on consolidating the cliff or trucking ammonia, and moving production elsewhere was 'not an option'. Which bias does the lecture name?
o: Framing
Sunk cost
Anchoring
Social conformity
quiz.e: How the problem was framed (keep production at Safi) limited the options; a study showed that moving ammonia production to Jorf removed the risk and generated more profit.

quiz.q: Which bias is 'the tendency to give disproportionate weight to the first piece of information'?
o: Anchoring
Framing
Confirmation bias
Sunk cost
quiz.e: Anchoring. Framing is about how a problem is posed, confirmation bias about favoring information that fits prior beliefs, and sunk cost about justifying earlier decisions.

written.q: OCP in 2006: diagnose the company's situation using the lecture's evidence, explain which cognitive biases blocked change (with an example), and show how analytics maps onto the four tiers of digital transformation, distinguishing Type 1 from Type 2 change.
written.m: Diagnosis: OCP (phosphate rock → phosphoric acid → fertilizers) was a state office until 2006, with an export royalty that gave the government shareholder poor incentives. Shareholder equity and net income deteriorated over 1995–2005, and the internal pension fund was described as 'a ticking bomb'. In 2007 it held ~45% of rock and ~46% of acid trade but under 10% of fertilizers, while traded phosphate shifted from raw rock toward processed products and 96% of new projects were integrated, so its downstream presence was weak. Kroll found no corruption, just an aging company with depreciating infrastructure and no real industrial and commercial strategy. Biases: pushback against 'strategic retreat' reflects pain-avoiding psychological denial (avoiding discomfort regardless of value). At Safi, decades of options (consolidating the cliff, trucking ammonia) reflect framing; a study showed that moving ammonia production to Jorf removed the risk and generated more profit. Analytics by tier: tiers 1–2 (operational and advanced operational efficiencies) include business steering through a daily multi-period MILP (~600,000 constraints, 500,000 variables, 60,000 binary), shipping optimization and demand and price prediction; these are Type 1 changes within the existing representation, reached by deduction. Tiers 3–4 (data-driven services and products) include digital agriculture, where $1 LIBS soil tests and 0.4-acre mapping replace 2.5-acre prescriptions that misdose ~40% of a field, and digital plant-nutrition services. These are Type 2 changes: a new business logic (selling customized nutrition and services, not tonnes of rock) reached by induction, which is uncertain and requires leaders to overcome the biases above.
k: State office, export royalty, poor incentives
Pain-avoiding denial; framing at Safi → Jorf
Tiers 1–2: MILP business steering, shipping, forecasting = Type 1
Tiers 3–4: digital agriculture, LIBS, TerraBlaster = Type 2
Induction is uncertain; change must be led

written.q: Explain why the economics of intangibles call for a different mindset than the economics of tangibles. Cover diminishing vs increasing returns, network effects (Metcalfe, data network effect) and how lower transaction costs change firm boundaries (Coase, Porter). Include a quantitative illustration.
written.m: Tangibles have positive marginal cost, economies of scale up to capacity limits, and diminishing returns. In Marshall's world unit cost is U-shaped in scale, so there is an optimal plant size, several firms coexist, prices track cost, and a predictable equilibrium of prices and shares emerges. Intangibles (information and data goods) have near-zero marginal cost, are non-rival and scalable, and show increasing returns: unit cost tends to zero as users grow, producing winner-takes-all, monopoly-like structures (Arthur, 1996). Network effects reinforce this: by Metcalfe's law value ∝ $n^2$, so tripling users from 1M to 3M multiplies network value by 9, not 3. The data network effect adds a loop: more usage → more data → better knowledge of patterns and preferences (e.g. collaborative filtering) → better products → more usage. Value also moves up the experience ladder: Starbucks turns $0.07 of beans into a $4.50 latte, about 64×. Firm boundaries change too. Coase: firms exist because using the market is costly, so the boundary sits where the marginal cost of organizing internally equals that of transacting with the market. Porter's value chain and five forces quietly assume high transaction costs; connectivity, open standards and AI agents cut them, moving the boundary toward fewer in-house activities and deconstructing value chains into platforms and ecosystems. As Arthur put it, the two worlds differ in behavior, style, culture, management, strategy and regulation, so they require different understandings, i.e. mindsets. Managers who apply tangible-world assumptions (cost-based pricing, capacity planning, fixed industry boundaries) to data businesses will misjudge strategy.

Marshall: optimal size, several firms, cost-based prices, equilibrium
Intangibles: near-zero marginal cost, non-rival, increasing returns, winner takes all
Metcalfe n² with a calculation (e.g. 3× users → 9× value)

Lower transaction costs → boundary moves, platforms/ecosystems
